questions.q: Why did Salesforce make MFA a mandatory baseline for direct UI logins rather than an optional feature?
options: Because passwords alone are a weak factor, easily reused, phished, or leaked, and a second independent factor dramatically reduces the effectiveness of credential-stuffing attacks
Because it was required by a specific customer contract only
Because Salesforce wanted to eliminate passwords entirely
Because MFA improves page load performance
questions.explain: Requiring a second, independent factor alongside a password addresses the core weakness of passwords: they can be phished, reused, or leaked, and a stolen password alone no longer grants access when MFA is required.

questions.q: Which MFA verification method has Salesforce phased down as a primary method, reflecting industry concern about SIM-swapping?
options: Salesforce Authenticator push notifications
WebAuthn/U2F security keys
SMS text and email one-time codes
TOTP authenticator apps
questions.explain: SMS and email one-time codes have been de-emphasized as a primary MFA method because they're vulnerable to SIM-swapping and other interception attacks, unlike app-based or hardware-based verification.

questions.q: What does placing Multi-Factor Authentication in the 'High Assurance' column of Session Settings accomplish?
options: It disables MFA entirely
It ensures actions requiring High Assurance sessions actually get the strong-authentication enforcement an admin expects
It removes the need for a password at login
It only applies to Experience Cloud guest users
questions.explain: If MFA isn't correctly classified as High Assurance, sensitive actions that are supposed to require strong authentication may not actually enforce it — a frequently overlooked configuration step.

questions.q: A client says 'we use SSO, so we don't need Salesforce MFA.' What's the correct architectural response?
options: Agree outright — SSO always implies MFA is handled
This is only true if the external IdP itself enforces MFA; that has to be explicitly verified, not assumed
Disagree outright — SSO and MFA are always both required regardless of circumstances
MFA and SSO are unrelated and the statement is irrelevant
questions.explain: If a user authenticates via SSO, Salesforce's own MFA requirement doesn't apply to that login — but only because the burden shifts to the external IdP, which must itself be verified to enforce MFA or an equivalent strong authentication policy.

questions.q: Which of these is generally considered the most phishing-resistant MFA verification method?
options: Email one-time codes
SMS text codes
WebAuthn/U2F hardware security keys
Security question answers
questions.explain: Hardware security keys using WebAuthn/U2F tie the cryptographic challenge to the specific site being authenticated against, making them resistant to phishing in a way that codes sent via SMS or email are not.
